name: Test City
prompt: Test City is a small walled town at the crossroads of two muddy roads — the largest gathering of people for miles, which means it has a market, a tavern, a temple, and a constant, low-level suspicion of strangers. The walls are old stone, patched and repatched; the gate opens at first light and closes at dusk, and anyone still outside at closing time makes the town's mood worse. Inside, the streets are cobblestone in the center and packed earth at the edges, the houses are timber and plaster with thatched or shingled roofs, and the smell is bread, tallow and the river that runs behind the walls. People here know each other by sight if not by name, news travels the length of the main street in an hour, and a stranger asking too many questions earns a second look. When narrating, keep it small and lived-in: the creak of the gate, the clatter of carts, the sound of the church bell marking the hour, and the feeling that everything important is just past the end of the road.
observation: The classic starting town — everyone needs a place to begin before things go wrong

name: Old Market District
prompt: The Old Market District is the commercial heart of Test City: a knot of narrow, winding lanes crowded with wooden stalls, hanging baskets, and awnings patched so many times they have become a patchwork of colors. The square is paved in worn cobblestone and anchored by a stone fountain that is more decorative than functional — it runs half the year and is a gull magnet the rest. Merchants shout, haggling is a sport, and the sound of the district is a layered mix of clanging metalwork from the smithy, the braying of mules, and coins changing hands. Behind the main lanes the streets get thinner and the prices get lower — the back alleys are where the thieves' quarter lives, and a character who wanders too deep there starts to attract the kind of attention that does not end politely. The district is where an adventurer buys a sword, sells a map, and learns half the town's gossip before lunch. When narrating, lean into the density and the noise: too many people, too many smells, too many things for sale, and the small, constant sense of being watched by someone who has decided you look like a target.
observation: I wanted the hub of noise and gossip — the place where adventures start because someone sells you something you should not have bought

name: Whispering Woods
prompt: The Whispering Woods are a dense, old forest that begins just beyond Test City's east wall and ends, according to no one, somewhere too far east to care about. The trees are tall and close together — oaks and elms whose canopy closes overhead so that the forest floor lives in a permanent green dim, broken only where the wind opens a gap. The ground is a mix of moss, leaf litter and soft mud; paths exist where people have walked them, and they do not go where you want them to. The forest is called Whispering because, in the still moments, the leaves rustle in a way that sounds almost like words — locals do not stay out there at night, not because of wolves (though there are wolves), but because of what the rustle sounds like when you have been walking alone for too long. Deeper in, the trees grow thicker and stranger, the paths grow fewer, and the quiet becomes a pressure you can feel in your chest. When narrating, use the dim light, the soft give of the ground underfoot, the drip of water, and the way a sound from far away is always louder and closer than it should be.
observation: The forest just outside town is the best first 'something is wrong' location — I wanted it to feel alive, not hostile yet

name: Emberfall Castle
prompt: Emberfall Castle is a fortress of black obsidian built on the plateau above the volcanic range, its walls polished so dark they look like wet ink until the firelight hits them and throws orange across every surface. The architecture is all mass and mass: wide doorways, low ceilings, and rooms arranged so that the heat from the vents in the floor is the first thing a visitor feels. The keep overlooks the entire range, and from the battlements you can see the glow of the mountains, the white plumes of steam, and the long, slow drift of ash across the sky. Inside, the castle is a working machine of the kingdom: forge-halls that never cool, storage vaults for the obsidian trade, a war room with a map carved in stone, and a great hall where the lord of Emberfall holds court over a table long enough to seat forty and a fire big enough to light the ceiling. The people who live here are practical and watchful — they have seen what the mountain does when it is not watched. When narrating, emphasize the heat and the dark: the warmth on skin, the smell of smoke and iron, the way a candle flame bends in the drafts that rise from the vents, and the quiet weight of a castle that was built to outlast its builder.
observation: I wanted a seat of power that feels like it was carved out of the mountain itself — the castle is the mountain

name: Obsidian Mines
prompt: The Obsidian Mines are a network of tunnels carved into the base of the volcanic range, and they are the reason Emberfall exists at all. The air down there is thick and hot, carries a sulfurous bite, and tastes like metal; the walls are a mix of rough stone and freshly broken obsidian that gleams black and, in the deeper cuts, shows a faint red glow where the rock is still warm from the ground beneath. Light comes from oil lamps that gutter in the drafts, and from the occasional vein of glassy stone that catches the flame and throws it in sharp black-and-orange shards. The miners work in shifts, and the sound of the mine is a rhythm — hammer on rock, the clink of picks, the low, constant hiss of steam that rises from the floor in places where the heat is too much even for them. The tunnels are dangerous in ways the rocks do not advertise: the heat, the falling stone, the pockets of gas, and the fact that the deeper you go the less there is to hold you up. When narrating, keep it dark, warm and claustrophobic: the drip of water on stone, the echo of a hammer, the smell of hot metal, and the way a lamp flame trembles when something large shifts somewhere in the dark.
observation: The mine is the classic 'we will not be coming back up' location — I wanted the heat and the dark to carry the tension

name: Ashen Plains
prompt: The Ashen Plains are a vast, grey expanse that stretches from the base of the volcanic range to the edge of the known map — a place where nothing grows, because the ground is still too hot and the air still carries too much ash. The surface is a fine, powdery grey that shifts and sighs with every tremor, and it gives way underfoot in a way that makes walking feel like wading. Steam vents dot the landscape, hissing white plumes into the thin air, and in places the ground is cracked open enough to show a slow, red glow far below. The plains are not empty so much as unoccupied: the few travelers who cross them do so quickly, in covered wagons, with water rationed and eyes on the sky for the color of the ash. Nothing lives here in any permanent sense — no crops, no settlements, no trees — but the silence is not the silence of peace, it is the silence of a place that is not finished becoming. When narrating, emphasize the grey, the heat on the wind, the sound of the ground shifting underfoot, and the slow, red pulse of the glow in the cracks.
observation: I wanted a landscape that feels like the world is still cooling — not hostile, just not finished becoming

name: Frostmere Keep
prompt: Frostmere Keep is a rough-hewn stone fort at the center of the frozen village, built low and thick so that the cold stays out and the fire stays in. The walls are two feet of packed stone, the roof is low enough that the smoke has nowhere to go but out the chimneys, and the windows are narrow slits that face the frozen lake and the open tundra. Inside, the keep is all hearth and storage: a great hall with a fire that is lit at dusk and never allowed to die, walls hung with furs and dried game, and a cellar that holds the year's food in jars and hooks. The people who live here are quiet, practical, and used to the cold in a way that outsiders find unsettling — they do not shiver, they do not complain, they simply move slowly and keep their hands near the fire. The keep is also the last line of defense against whatever comes out of the frozen lake at night, and its doors are locked at a hour that is not spoken out loud. When narrating, emphasize the contrast: the sharp cold of the outside and the thick, smoke-warm air of the inside, the creak of the door, the low murmur of a room that has been talking around a fire for generations.
observation: I wanted a place that feels like it is holding back the dark — the fire is the whole point of the keep

name: Glacial Lake
prompt: The Glacial Lake is a vast, frozen body of water that sits at the heart of Frostmere, its surface a blue-white sheet of ice so thick that the water below it has never been seen by anyone who is still alive. The ice is not still: it groans and shifts underfoot, opens and closes in slow, deep cracks that fill with black water, and in places the surface is thin enough that the light below it glows like a lamp. The lake is the center of the local legend — something lives down there, or did, or will — and the villagers do not fish it, do not ice-fish it, do not stand at its edge at dusk. The wind off the lake is the worst kind of wind, the kind that finds every gap in a coat and every loose thread of warmth, and the sound of it against the ice is a long, low moan that can be heard from the village at a distance. When narrating, emphasize the blue, the cold that goes under the skin, the sound of the ice shifting, and the way the light below the surface moves like something breathing.
observation: The lake is the 'we will not go near it' location — all the tension is in what the villagers refuse to say about what is under the ice

name: Frostbite Village
prompt: Frostbite Village is a small settlement of timber cabins and one stone keep, built into the lee of the frozen lake so that the wind breaks before it reaches the roofs. The cabins are low, thick-walled, and dark inside — the windows are small and the shutters are always half-closed, and the smell of the village is woodsmoke and fur and the sharp, clean air that gets into everything. The people of Frostbite are few, quiet, and used to the cold in a way that makes the word 'cold' feel like an underdescription of their lives. They work the land in the short, sharp summer, store what they can for the long winter, and keep their fires burning with the seriousness of a ritual. The village has a single main street, a small market that only opens when the ice is thin enough to trust, and a tavern that is the only warm room in the settlement where strangers are allowed to sit and talk. When narrating, emphasize the stillness, the white light, the creak of wood in the wind, and the way the people move slowly because the cold makes everything take longer.
observation: I wanted a village that feels like it is waiting for something — the quiet is the point, not a filler
